details:
**Of Grammatology**
Derrida's 1967 book, the founding text of deconstruction and the most common giveaway for him. It argues that Western philosophy has privileged speech over writing, treating writing as a secondary copy of speech. Its English translation by Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak features the Egyptian god of writing, Thoth, on the cover.

**Deconstruction**
The method of reading that Derrida pioneered. It shows that apparently neutral binary oppositions in a text (speech/writing, presence/absence, nature/culture) are actually hierarchies that privilege one term, and then reveals how the text itself undermines and destabilizes that hierarchy.

**Speech privileged over writing (logocentrism and phonocentrism)**
Derrida's central critique of Western metaphysics. He argued that philosophers since Plato have treated speech as closer to truth and presence and writing as a mere derivative, and he called this privileging of the spoken word and of a fixed rational meaning (logos) "logocentrism."

**"There is nothing outside the text"**
Derrida's famous claim from Of Grammatology (in French, "il n'y a pas de hors-texte"). It means that there is no meaning free of the context and play of language, and it was often mocked by critics such as John Searle.

**Différance**
Derrida's coined term, spelled with an "a" so that it is pronounced the same as the French "différence" and can only be distinguished in writing. It combines "to differ" and "to defer," expressing that a sign's meaning depends on its difference from other signs and is always postponed, never fully present.

**Rousseau and the "logic of supplementarity"**
The second half of Of Grammatology analyzes Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Essay on the Origin of Languages. Derrida shows that Rousseau treats writing as a "supplement" to speech, something both added on and filling in a lack, and that this logic undermines Rousseau's claim that speech is natural and complete.

**Saussure**
The first half of Of Grammatology critiques the linguist Ferdinand de Saussure, who claimed that writing exists for the sole purpose of representing speech. Derrida turns Saussure's own idea that signs gain meaning only through difference against this privileging of speech.

**John Searle and Limited Inc**
Derrida criticized J. L. Austin's speech-act theory in "Signature Event Context," and Searle replied attacking his reading. Derrida answered in "Limited Inc a b c...," and the debate was collected in the book Limited Inc, but Searle refused permission to reprint his reply in it. Searle accused Derrida of deliberate obscurantism.

**Iterability**
Derrida's concept, central to the Searle debate, that any sign must be repeatable in new contexts in order to function as a sign. This means that its meaning can never be fully fixed by an original context or by the speaker's intention.

**"Structure, Sign, and Play in the Discourse of the Human Sciences"**
Derrida's 1966 lecture at Johns Hopkins University, which helped launch post-structuralism in America. It argues that Western thought has organized structures around a fixed "center" (such as God, Man, or essence), describes a "rupture" that decentered this thinking, and calls for embracing "free play." It also says that Nietzsche, Freud, and Heidegger "destroy each other reciprocally."

**"Plato's Pharmacy"**
Derrida's essay, collected in Dissemination, on Plato's Phaedrus. It focuses on the Greek word pharmakon, which can mean both "remedy" and "poison," and which Plato applies to writing in the myth of Theuth (Thoth) presenting writing to the king Thamus.

**Transcendental signified**
Derrida's term for a supposed ultimate meaning or concept, outside the system of signs, to which all signs finally point. He argued that no such final anchor exists, so meaning keeps sliding from signifier to signifier.

**Writing and Difference**
Derrida's 1967 essay collection, published the same year as Of Grammatology. It includes "Structure, Sign, and Play" and "Cogito and the History of Madness," his critique of Michel Foucault's reading of Descartes in History of Madness, which led to a long dispute with Foucault.

**Specters of Marx**
Derrida's 1993 book on the legacy of Marxism after the fall of the Soviet Union. It introduces "hauntology," lists ten "plagues" of the new world order of global capitalism, and calls for a "New International."

**Cambridge honorary degree controversy**
In 1992 a proposal to give Derrida an honorary degree at Cambridge University provoked protest, including a letter signed by Willard Van Orman Quine and other philosophers claiming his work "does not meet accepted standards of clarity and rigour." The degree was approved after a vote. Derrida also drew controversy for defending his late colleague Paul de Man after de Man's wartime pro-Nazi journalism was discovered.
